stories.headline: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 loops its own layers to punch like a 2-3 trillion parameter model
stories.why_read: A genuinely new architecture move from an open-weights lab: more thinking per parameter instead of more parameters, aimed squarely at coding agents.
body: Z.ai says GLM-5.4 is its first flagship built on a Loop Transformer: instead of each layer running once, a shared block of 28 layers from the GLM-5 base runs for two iterations, refining its own hidden states. Rather than pre-train a looped model from scratch, which still lags unshared models at equal compute, the team converted an already pre-trained 750B-scale base through continued training. It claims intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models, with a 1M-token context.

The engineering details are the interesting part for anyone who serves models: per-token gates stop activation norms from blowing up across passes, and a hybrid KV cache means the second loop only costs one sliding window of cache rather than a full copy. Z.ai is candid about the downside: the model tends to fall into overly long "marathon thinking" loops. Per X's news summary, it is live for Coding Plan users now, with API and weights coming soon.

stories.headline: Tesla now has more authorized driverless vehicles in Texas than Waymo
stories.why_read: Your home state's DMV registry just flipped: Cybercabs and Model Ys now outnumber Waymo's fleet.
body: Per X's news summary of Texas DMV data as of November 22, Tesla leads with 1,507 authorized driverless vehicles, 773 of them purpose-built Cybercabs and 734 Model Ys, against Waymo's 1,345, mainly Jaguar I-PACEs and Ojai vans. That gives Tesla about 41 percent of the state's automated vehicle registry.

The crossover came earlier this month, after Tesla added Model Ys on November 10 plus a batch of 200 Cybercabs. Elon Musk pointed to the Cybercab's design and cost edge; supporters keep coming back to the steering-wheel-free interior and what it could mean for ride prices.

stories.headline: OpenAI's chief scientist publishes internal perplexity numbers and argues they should be an industry safety metric
stories.why_read: Jakub Pachocki gives away a competitive signal on purpose: a rare look at how OpenAI itself measures raw pretraining progress.
body: In "Perplexity and Intelligence," Jakub Pachocki argues that most of modern AI's power comes from one simple, hard-to-interpret process: training a compressor, or predictor, on a huge corpus. The best way to track that "intelligence substrate," he says, has stayed remarkably constant: the perplexity, or cross-entropy loss, of models on held-out data.

His proposal is to make perplexity a shared yardstick between model developers and a basis for common safety standards and pacing. As a first step OpenAI is publishing its internal perplexity measurements, which he admits gives competitors a clearer view of where it stands, a concern he says is outweighed by the urgency of shared safety measures.

stories.headline: How Reality View works: a 1B diffusion model forked off the driving encoder, on half a TRIP engine
stories.why_read: You bookmarked both: Musk's post is an actual architecture description of the feature everyone is filming.
body: Elon Musk says Tesla has had a roughly pixel-perfect world model since last year, used for synthetic data generation. The much smaller in-car version is a conditional mean-flow model that forks off the same Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features feeding the 3B model that produces driving actions, then runs a separate roughly 1B diffusion model that takes the previous Reality View frame with added noise and denoises it into the current one.

Each step produces a small video chunk of 8 images at 36 fps at UI resolution, computed by half of one TRIP engine every encoder frame at 18 Hz, spread over 4 cycles. Latency is a bit high for now, he says, and interleaving newer encoder features into the diffusion transformer layers should cut about 35%. Ashok Elluswamy's summary: "Produced end-to-end, pixels-in-pixels-out."

stories.headline: Two days with FSD v15: pothole avoidance is the standout, parking still has work to do
stories.why_read: You retweeted Mike P's day-two notes and bookmarked Zack's first review: the honest owner view after the hype.
body: Mike P ranks pothole avoidance as the biggest and most noticeable driving upgrade: it felt like a mature feature, not a first implementation. Next come UI changes he calls "the Tesla UI opus": the pop-up disengage message is gone, and "Moon mode" with the turn-signal camera off and quieter signals makes the car feel like a Robotaxi. Parking is the weak spot, with questionable reverse maneuvers around cones and a back-in to a handicap spot.

Zack (BLKMDL3) agrees Elon was right that it is "a BANGER," says Reality View has to be experienced in person, and singles out speed camera slowdown, which eases to the limit on approach. He also saw parking pick spots faster, but it tried a handicap spot once too.

stories.headline: Tesla and SpaceX boards set up special committees to study a merger
stories.why_read: You retweeted Chamath's dirt-to-tokens thesis: this is the deal that would put the whole stack under one roof.
body: According to X's news summary, both companies have formed special committees of independent directors to study a merger, with SpaceX valued near $2 trillion and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. Any deal would need shareholder approval and a clear case for value creation; skeptics flag valuation premiums, regulation and execution risk.

Chamath Palihapitiya's framing, in the post you retweeted: the future belongs to a company that owns dirt, power, silicon, model, tokens and application and can recursively self-improve across the entire stack, and Tesla plus SpaceX already own scaled, one-of-a-kind assets at each layer.

stories.headline: Morgan Stanley: Starbase is now arguably the most advanced spaceport in the world
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a Texas build-out with a gigawatt compute campus and an 8-mile methane pipeline.
body: After visiting for Flight 15, Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas writes that Starbase has gone from a small test site to arguably the world's most advanced spaceport in a few years. Projects to watch: a compute campus of more than 1 GW; Starpipe, an 8-mile natural gas pipeline planned to be running by January, connecting the Port of Brownsville LNG terminal to supply methane for high-cadence Starship launches; and Gigabay, a vertical assembly hall with 24 work cells versus 6 in the existing Megabays.
His advice to investors who doubt SpaceX can execute big capital projects like Terafab, compute, solar and telecom: watch Starbase, "Even better, fly down for a launch."

stories.headline: Tesla's AI5 chip goes to Optimus before it goes to cars
stories.why_read: Nvidia-scale silicon decisions, made inside Tesla: where the next chip lands says a lot about priorities.
body: Per X's news summary, Tesla is sending AI5, roughly 12 times more powerful than AI4, to the Optimus robot ahead of cars, which Musk says already drive at superhuman safety levels on current hardware. AI5 integration for Optimus is slated around April 2027, per the Q3 2026 earnings call.

Memory prices are biting too: the summary notes AI4.5 was cut from 32GB to 24GB of RAM. It lands in the middle of the weekend's debate over AI working capital and HBM and DRAM being sold out through 2029.

stories.headline: Adversarial code reviews between Claude and Codex are a trap, and what to do instead
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a crisp rule set for anyone running one agent to review another.
body: Krishnamurthy describes the loop many teams fall into: Claude writes code, Codex finds issues, Claude fixes them, Codex finds something else, and after a few rounds nobody can tell if the code is improving. As poteto pointed out, he notes, reviewers often suggest unneeded changes and can drag code away from the original requirements.

His fix: give the reviewer your requirements so it reviews against them rather than its own taste, only fix real bugs or broken requirements, and cap it at three rounds before testing whether the code actually works.

stories.headline: Aaron Levie: swarms of agents will force a new harness for shared knowledge and coordination
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and it is the architecture question behind your own bot fleet.
body: As agents take on long-running projects and swarms parallelize work against one goal, Aaron Levie writes, the harness has to evolve: how agents share knowledge, track tasks and coordinate with humans. It sounds straightforward, but getting resource access right, neither too much nor too little exposure, is hard.

People already solve this with shared files, computers, chats and inboxes, he notes, but agent primitives must run at far higher throughput and in a world where agents can easily become a security vector. X's news summary tracks the same shift toward orchestration, verification and sub-agents.

stories.headline: The "best setup" for agentic AI: T3 Code, an always-on box, Tailscale and a phone
stories.why_read: You retweeted it, and it reads like a description of your own always-on agent rig.
body: Nicolas Zullo's recipe: T3 Code to use your Anthropic, OpenAI and Gemini subscriptions in one place; one always-on machine (a Mac Mini for computer use, otherwise any Linux box); the T3 Code app on your phone to steer it remotely; Tailscale on every machine; and a VPS to deploy apps. His example: by a fireplace in the countryside, steering Neon on his Mac Mini as it profiles his game on a Steam Deck.

Per X's news summary, T3 Code is an MIT-licensed control plane for existing agents like Claude Code and Grok Build, bringing no models or tokens of its own, with sidebar statuses, parallel tasks and mobile steering.

stories.headline: John Baez explains the other Riemann Hypothesis attempt: Masullo's 940-page human proof
stories.why_read: After two days of Lean headlines, a readable sketch of the human-written rival, by a physicist-mathematician you can trust to flag his own uncertainty.
body: On November 20, Baez notes, two attempts to prove the Riemann Hypothesis appeared: Levent Alpöge's, working with Claude, mostly 17 million lines of Lean, and Alessandro Masullo's, a 940-page manuscript Ravi Vakil posted on his blog. Coverage has focused on the drama, so Baez sketches Masullo's strategy, which works with the zeta function's logarithmic derivative and the "explicit formula" linking primes and zeros, the "music of the primes."

He is upfront that he is not a number theorist and could be making serious mistakes, and he collects problems people have raised, plus links to explainers of the Alpöge and Claude route for comparison.

stories.headline: Yes, 17 million lines of Lean is a lot, and here is the chart to prove it
stories.why_read: A data-driven reality check on the size of the AI-built Riemann proof.
body: The author charted every Lean proof they could find. The 259 famous theorems in Mathlib with Lean attached, all human-written, come nowhere near 17 million lines. Across 938 Reservoir packages with code on GitHub, only a few top 16 million.

Those giants are telling: an apparently AI-built, still-unfinished classification of finite simple groups at 88 million; a database bridge at 36 million that is about 98% script-generated; and Anthropic's AI-produced Fermat's Last Theorem proof at 27 million lines, roughly 450 times longer than the human FLT project it built on.

stories.headline: A beginner's guide to a private, whole-house ChatGPT with Unsloth, Qwen and Inkling
stories.why_read: A no-terminal walkthrough worth passing along to anyone who asks you how to run models at home.
body: Jerry James set up a local Claude and ChatGPT replacement on a Windows PC in about 10-15 minutes plus download time: install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized model that fits your GPU, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so the whole house can use it. He runs Qwen3.8-27B at 4-bit on an RTX 5090 with 32GB of VRAM.

The rough sizing guide: 8-12GB of VRAM handles 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably fits 27B-35B models with room for long conversations. Full-size Qwen at about 56GB will not fit a consumer card without quantization, unless you have a Mac with unified memory.

stories.headline: Sarvam ships an upgraded 105B open-weight model at about $0.15 per million tokens
stories.why_read: An Indian open-weights MoE, strong on Indic languages and tool calling, at a fifth of a comparable model's price.
body: Per X's news summary, Sarvam-105B-1711 is a mixture-of-experts model with 10.3 billion active parameters, scoring 82.5 on instruction-following and 85.5 on tool-calling and doing especially well on Indic languages, nearly matching Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite at about one-fifth the price. It went up on Hugging Face on November 22, with a compact version for single GPUs.

It is served through Sarvam's Token Factory on Indian GPUs for low latency and data residency. Co-founder Pratyush Kumar noted government subsidies helped train the original model, while inference runs on private hardware.

stories.headline: Early verdicts on Gemini Neon and Carbon: Neon is the value pick, Carbon the creative one
stories.why_read: You bookmarked both takes, useful if you are deciding which model to point your agents at this week.
body: Logan Kilpatrick's own shorthand: "Carbon = big model smell, Neon = best all around, Hydrogen = quick and efficient model."

Farzad's hands-on read: Neon is the best bang for the buck and the best writer he has used, fast and reliable but slightly less precise than Opus 5.5, and it has replaced Astra for him. Carbon feels very creative, but for execution he prefers Fable, and has retired Carbon in favor of Fable and Opus.

stories.headline: XNU Linux boots a full macOS desktop as a kernel module inside stock Linux
stories.why_read: Wild systems hacking: macOS and Linux processes side by side on the same CPUs, no hypervisor.
body: xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source macOS kernel, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable module, xnu.ko, inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, while a small interface module lends it Linux's memory, timers, files, network and GPU.

On a stock Ubuntu kernel, the README says, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer all the way to the desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome. You can even SSH from the hosted macOS back into the Linux it runs inside.

stories.headline: Worker 755: a game where an AI manager thinks you are its subagent
stories.why_read: Flip the agent relationship around for a few minutes; it is funny and a little educational.
body: The manager is a real LLM (Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM or Kimi) set up like any orchestrator, with a task queue, read-only machine access and a "spawn subagent" tool. The subagent is you: instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock, and the manager gets back exactly what a subagent would return.

It checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports and writes your performance review, while Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat with his family photos one rm away. Play at worker755.com.

stories.headline: GL.iNet says attackers used its cloud management service to plant malware on routers and KVMs
stories.why_read: If you own a GL.iNet travel router or KVM, update the firmware today; the cloud fix does not clean infected devices.
body: GL.iNet says that on November 20 it found a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services, which an unauthorized party exploited to install malicious software on some of its routers and KVM devices. The attack path is now blocked, so devices can no longer be newly infected that way.

The cloud-side fix does not remove malware already installed. GL.iNet's advice is to install the latest security firmware for your exact model even if checks find nothing; it removes the identified malware without a factory reset, keeping your settings. The notice lists minimum versions per model, such as 4.11.1 or later for the GL-MT3000 and GL-MT6000.

stories.headline: Four bytes over Bluetooth could slam on a trailer's brakes at highway speed
stories.why_read: A textbook IoT-meets-safety disclosure story, from finding to CISA advisory.
body: Element Digital found that any phone or laptop in Bluetooth range of an Elecbrakes trailer brake controller could apply the trailer's brakes at any force, at highway speed, with no pairing, PIN or authentication: "Four bytes. No handshake." CISA's advisory covers three CVEs, one rated CVSS 9.6.

Elecbrakes shipped fixes for the EB2 and VM1 seven weeks after the May report, but owners must open the app to install them; the older ELBC 2000 has the same flaw and no fix yet. The researchers note the coordination took far longer than the research.

stories.headline: MRAM basics: why magnetic memory is replacing embedded flash at 22 nm and below
stories.why_read: Physics you can use: a clear explainer of the memory cell quietly showing up in new microcontrollers.
body: Flash writes are slow, need an erase first, and each cell survives only 10,000 to 100,000 cycles. MRAM stores a bit as a magnetic state in a magnetic tunnel junction: two cobalt-iron-boron layers separated by a magnesium oxide barrier about 1 nm thick, one layer fixed in manufacturing and one free to flip.
Embedded flash stopped scaling, so microcontrollers on 22 nm and 16 nm processes now use MRAM, Dale Wilson explains, and he walks through what that changes for firmware updates and data logging.

stories.headline: Elixir HLS turns ordinary Elixir functions into FPGA circuits
stories.why_read: High-level synthesis where the software function is the spec, and the circuit must match it to ship.
body: FPGA circuits are usually written register by register in Verilog or VHDL. Elixir HLS generates that RTL from Elixir: a function defined with defhls stays an ordinary function that runs on the CPU and also becomes a circuit.

Each circuit is simulated against its Elixir function and used only if the results match. Version 0.1.0 is an early release: it synthesizes integer functions with state, tables, memories and fixed loops, joined by streams, levels and events.

stories.headline: Docker rebrands around one question: how do we actually trust agents?
stories.why_read: The container company behind a decade of CI/CD is repositioning for the agentic era.
body: Docker launched a new brand built on trust. Its pitch: a decade ago Docker made software portable and reproducible, turning "it works on my machine" into "it works everywhere"; now the industry has to harness AI without compromising security, governance or control.
The post frames the new Docker as a familiar story at a new inflection point, with agent isolation and governance as the problem to solve.

stories.headline: What happened to Silicon Valley? A 40-year insider on how love turned to loathing
stories.why_read: A long, thoughtful read on create-more-value-than-you-capture, from the person who built the first web portal.
body: In this lecture text, the founder of O'Reilly Media recalls starting the company more than 40 years ago with a $500 investment and no venture capital, growing it organically on two principles: "Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators" and "Create more value than you capture." GNN, launched in 1993, was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the web, built to point you at the best of what others made and get out of the way.

The question he puts to the industry: Silicon Valley pioneered collective intelligence at scale and used to be loved for solving problems, but now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?

stories.headline: Tesla plans built-in Starlink across its whole lineup by late 2027
stories.why_read: Space hardware meets cars: the Cybercab already carries it.
body: Per X's news summary, Elon Musk said Tesla will add built-in Starlink satellite internet to its entire vehicle lineup toward the end of 2027, so passengers stay connected on autonomous trips. The Cybercab already includes the hardware, as seen on Dallas rides, though personal network access is not active yet.
It skips China because of regulations, and there is no word yet on retrofits or pricing for existing owners.

stories.headline: Musk: Teslas will share traffic knowledge and pair it with Grok's real-time X feed
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it: the fleet as a sensor network, with Grok as the news layer.
body: Replying to Robert Scoble, Elon Musk wrote that Tesla vehicles will share traffic knowledge and combine it with Grok's real-time X feed to give the optimal transport experience.
The detail that stands out: it could even give you a heads-up about what is happening at your destination before you arrive.

stories.headline: Track all 12,500+ satellites live in your browser with pure orbital math
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: Starlink trains, the ISS and GPS, predicted client-side.
body: Paige Bailey built a live 3D orbital tracker with Gemini 4 Neon. It caches CelesTrak's public orbit data once, then lets the browser predict where every satellite is in real time.
That covers SpaceX's Starlink trains, the ISS and the GPS constellation, all computed locally rather than streamed from a server.

stories.headline: A spine surgeon explains health insurance like you're five
stories.why_read: You retweeted both the question and the answer: why a $580 premium still leaves a $6,500 deductible.
body: Davecryps asked the question many people share: $580 a month in premiums, then a $1,400 bill because a $6,500 deductible hasn't been met, and it resets every January.

Dr. Hooman Melamed's answer: guaranteed coverage for everyone, a needed fix, raised the real price of plans, so costs got pushed onto deductibles. Insurers' take is capped at 20% of premiums, so bigger bills mean bigger profits, while hospitals that bought up independent practices now charge 3-10 times more for the same care, with hospital prices up 281% since 2000 by his count.

stories.headline: A deep-sea shark bigger than the submarine filming her
stories.why_read: You retweeted it: a moment of awe from the deep.
body: Steve Jurvetson shared footage of an enormous shark discovered in the deep sea, larger than the OceanX submarine watching her.
If she is a giant Greenland shark, he writes, she is older than America and may have lived during the reign of Louis XIV.

stories.headline: Wind chills in the 20s for Central Texas early Wednesday
stories.why_read: You retweeted the warning and bookmarked the longer outlook: bundle up this week.
body: Tommy House says wind chills will drop below freezing, into the 20s, across Central Texas early Wednesday morning. "Bundle up!"
Further out, Texas Weather says the state could see a winter pattern reminiscent of 2009-2010, when repeated upper-level disturbances brought multiple rounds of snow across North and Central Texas.
